## Motivation

It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a Ph.D. student in possession of a
stipend, must be in want of a raise.

Ph.D. programs vary widely between countries and disciplines, so it is hard to
generalize. But in many programs, Ph.D. students are funded: the university
covers the cost of their tuition and pays a modest stipend to cover the
student's living expenses. This stipend may require the student to do some work
outside their academic studies, such as serving as a teaching assistant for
courses, or it may pay them to conduct their thesis research. Nominally, this
pay is for about 20 hours of work a week, so it is not a full-time job even
though the student may spend much more than 40 hours a week on their academic
work.

Whatever the case, Ph.D. stipends are paid for from university funds, research
grants, fellowships, and other sources, and they are rarely generous. Stipends
are almost always lower than wages for jobs in the field, and are often below
what is considered a living wage. Students thus often argue for higher stipends.
There are many possible arguments---based on wages for comparable jobs, on
living wage standards, on the effect of low pay on mental and physical health,
and so on---but one possible argument is that improved pay may improve outcomes:

> This analysis looks at graduate student pay from another angle: that of
> program outcomes. Setting aside the debate over whether students *deserve*
> higher wages, there may be another reason for which student pay should be
> higher. If better wages lead to greater success, then this will be reflected
> in program outcomes, and higher-paying departments can reap reputational
> benefits as a result. (Warner and Stecuła, 2024)

This data comes from a study that aimed to answer this question. The authors
gathered data on 85 Ph.D. programs in political science in the United States,
including their number of graduates, program ranking, location, and outcomes:
how many graduates got tenure-track jobs. Stipends are often not listed
publicly, so they gathered self-reported data from PhDStipends.com, where
students can report the stipends they receive or were offered by Ph.D. programs.

## Data

The data is split into two files. One file contains one row per Ph.D. program,
giving metadata about the program. The other file contains one row per stipend
report on PhDStipends.com. Each program may have more than one reported stipend,
if more than one student reported it or if students reported stipends in
different years.

### Variable descriptions

| Variable | Description |
|----|-------------|
| program | Ph.D. program |
| stipend | Stipend amount (dollars) |
| coaiadj_pay | Ratio of stipend amount to county-level cost of living, as estimated by MIT Living Wage Lab (less than 1 = lower than cost of living) |
| acyear | Academic year stipend was reported |
| pryear | Student's year in their Ph.D. program |
| stipendnotes | Additional comments listed by the student in their submission |
: phd-stipends.csv

| Variable | Description |
|----|-------------|
| program | Ph.D. program |
| link | Link to the program's web page |
| listed | Whether the program's outcome data was available (1 = yes, 0 = no) |
| grads | Ph.D. graduates in the 2019-2021 academic years (if a list was publicly available) |
| ustenure | How many of those graduates obtained tenure-track jobs at US institutions during the 2019-2021 hiring cycles, as of January 2022 |
| alltenure | Same but for all institutions, not just US |
| non_tt | How many of those graduates obtained non-tenure-track academic jobs during the 2019-2021 hiring cycles, as of November 2023 |
| size | Number of Ph.D. students listed in the program's directory |
| rank13 | The program's rank in the 2013 US News and World Report program rankings (or 100 if the program was not ranked) |
| top_subfield | If the program was ranked in one of the political science subfields in the 2013 US News and World Report (1 = yes, 0 = no) |
| union | Whether the graduate students were unionized as of 2018 (1 = yes, 0 = no) |
| metro_rating | The size of the metro area in which the program is located (2 = top 20 metro areas by population, 1 = top 100, 0 = other) |
| endowment_fte | University's endowment divided by the number of full-time enrolled students |
| type | Whether the university is public or private |
| region | US Census region of the university |
: phd-programs.csv

## Questions

1. Determine how to merge the program and stipend information. How much do
   stipends vary within a program? Should you simply take the average stipend
   per program? Merge the data.
2. Conduct EDA. What is the typical Ph.D. stipend? Is it related to the
   program's rank, the cost of living, whether the university is public or
   private, or the region? Do universities with higher endowments (per student)
   pay better stipends? Devise plots or tables to address these questions.
3. The core question is whether better-paying programs have better outcomes, in
   terms of the fraction of students who get academic jobs. Select a model to
   answer this question. Can you find evidence for it?
4. The authors of the original study claim that according to their results, the
   stipend amount "clearly and meaningfully impacts their ability to thrive on
   the highly competitive job market". That is, they regard the association as
   indicating that stipends *cause* an increase in placement. Under what
   conditions can we make a causal claim? Are there confounding variables, or
   other variables we would need to measure?
